about.title: About Data Corn
about.how.title: How it works
about.how.text: You draw your field. We read 25 past seasons of weather for that spot from NASA and public sources, run a soil water model for each season, and show what happened. Each season is a scenario, not a forecast.
about.limits.title: What to keep in mind
about.limits.1: These are scenarios, not forecasts. Nobody can say what this season will do.
about.limits.2: When most data is missing, we show "not available". When soil or slope is missing, the engine uses generic values and lists them in the report's data sources.
about.limits.3: The model does not carry water between crops, and it has no yield records for your field.
about.limits.4: Data Corn supports farmers and agronomists. It does not replace their judgment or field scouting.
about.credits.title: Data credits
about.credits.nasa: NASA is a data source only. NASA does not endorse or review this project.
about.ai.title: Made with AI help
about.ai.chat: The optional chat assistant is SI too: a language model, reached through OpenRouter, that explains the example report's numbers. It reads them from the report and computes nothing, and it can be wrong.
chat.title: Ask about this report
chat.notice: SI assistant, it can be wrong.
chat.intro: Ask what a result means or how it was worked out. Answers use this report's numbers: scenarios from past seasons, not a forecast. You can attach one photo or one PDF per message.
chat.placeholder: For example: why is the water risk high?
chat.truncated: The answer was cut short. Ask for the rest.
chat.feedback.label: Was this answer useful?
chat.feedback.thanks: Thanks for your feedback. It does not include your question or the answer.
chat.feedback.failed: The feedback could not be sent.
chat.privacy: Your question and any file go to an AI service (OpenRouter) to answer it. Data Corn does not save them; closing the page clears the conversation.
chat.error.not_configured: The assistant is not set up on this server.
chat.error.rate_limited: Too many questions in a short time. Wait a few minutes and try again.
chat.error.unknown_report: The assistant only explains the example report computed in advance.
chat.error.report_unavailable: The report could not be read. Try again in a moment.
chat.error.body_too_large: The message is too large. Send a smaller file or a shorter conversation.
chat.error.bad_attachment_type: Attach a photo (JPEG, PNG or WebP) or a PDF.
chat.error.attachment_too_large: The file is larger than 2.5 MB, even after shrinking. Try a smaller one.
chat.error.model_error: The assistant could not answer. Try again.
chat.error.model_busy: The AI service is busy right now. Wait a minute and try again.
chat.error.too_many_tool_rounds: The assistant took too many steps. Ask a simpler question.
chat.error.network: The connection dropped. Check it and try again.

help.title: Help
help.faq.forecast.a: No. Data Corn reads 25 past seasons of weather for your field, runs a soil water model for each one and shows what happened. Each season is a scenario, not a forecast: nobody can say what this season will do.
help.faq.data.q: Where does the data come from?
help.faq.data.a: Weather comes from NASA POWER and El Niño from NOAA; for fields in the US, soil comes from USDA NRCS SSURGO and past crops from the USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer. The data credits are under “{about}”. NASA is a data source only; it does not endorse or review this project.
help.faq.sample.a: The public demo runs without a data server. “{example}” opens a field in Nebraska with real results calculated ahead of time for each irrigation choice ({none}, {pivot}, {furrow} or {drip}), if you leave the other details as they are. Any other field or change shows made-up sample numbers with that tag.
help.faq.pdf.q: The PDF did not download. What can I do?
help.faq.pdf.a: When the PDF is ready, a line appears under the button: tap “{open}” to open the same file. Inside Instagram, Facebook or TikTok the download may be blocked: open this page in Safari or Chrome.
help.faq.account.q: Do I need an account? What do you keep about me?
help.faq.account.a: No. Data Corn has no login and no accounts, and it does not ask for your name or email. Your “{display}” choices (text size, contrast, calm mode) stay in this browser.
help.faq.draw.q: How do I draw my field?
help.faq.draw.a: Use “{locate}” or “{search}”, then tap each corner of your field on the map; drag a corner to move it, and “{undo}” removes the last one. Tap the first point or “{close}” to finish. The field needs at least 3 corners, sides that do not cross, and 1 to 2,000 ha (about 2.5 to 4,900 acres).
help.faq.risk.q: What do the risk levels mean?
help.faq.risk.a: Each card shows a level as a symbol and a word: {low_icon} {low}, {medium_icon} {medium}, {high_icon} {high}, or {no_data_icon} {no_data} when data is missing. The level comes from the analysis of your field. “{hybrid}” shows the higher of its two levels, and “{rotation}” shows {low} when the last crop on record is the one the rotation suggests, {medium} when it is not.
help.suggestion.text: What would make Data Corn more useful on your farm? Tell us: a missing option, a confusing word or a new idea.
help.support.text: Something not working? Tell us what you did and what happened.
help.support.device: Please say which device and browser you used, for example “Android phone, Chrome”.
help.github_signin: GitHub asks you to sign in with a free GitHub account before you post.

summary.good: Most past seasons went well on this field. Plant between {start_date} and {end_date}.
rotation.soy_first: Corn after soybean fits here. In this field's history: {after_soy} years after soybean and {after_corn} after corn.
rotation.corn_on_slopes: With this slope and conventional tillage, soybean's thin residue raises erosion. Here corn after corn protects the soil better.
rotation.note.rootworm: Rotating breaks the corn rootworm cycle.
rotation.note.residue: Corn leaves more residue: it protects the soil but keeps it cooler at planting.
rotation.panel.title: Three ways to rotate
rotation.panel.intro: Scenarios, not forecasts. Each one shows what we know, what we don't, and what to check locally.
rotation.no_carryover: The model does not carry water between crops.
rotation.why.current: The crop map (USDA CDL) shows this pattern on this field in recent years.
rotation.strategy.continuous_corn.why: It grows the most corn each year. Shown to compare.
rotation.strategy.continuous_corn.eviden: In Iowa State plots from 2000 to 2007, corn after corn yielded from almost the same to 27% less than corn after soybean, 14% less on average. Source: Iowa State University Extension (Al-Kaisi and others).
rotation.strategy.continuous_corn.benefi: Corn every year. Corn leaves a lot of residue that covers the soil.
rotation.strategy.continuous_corn.unknow: How much yield this field loses after corn. We have no yield records for this field, and the model does not simulate it.
rotation.strategy.continuous_corn.risks: Corn rootworm and corn diseases can build up. Corn after corn needs 30 to 50 lb/acre more nitrogen (Iowa State).
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean.why: It is the rotation that extension trials compare with corn after corn. Shown to compare.
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean.evidence: In a 26-year Iowa State study (Nashua, 1979 to 2004), corn after soybean yielded 16 bu/acre more than corn after corn on average, from 0 to 40 by year. Source: Iowa State University Extension (Mallarino and Pecinovsky).
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean.benefits: A year without corn can break the corn rootworm cycle. Corn after soybean needs less nitrogen: continuous corn needs 30 to 50 lb/acre more (Iowa State).
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean.unknown: How much yield or nitrogen this field gains. We have no yield records for this field.
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean.risks: Soybean leaves little residue, so slopes erode more. Northern corn rootworm eggs can stay dormant for two or more winters, and some western corn rootworm lay eggs in soybean, so one year without corn may not be enough.
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean_rye: Corn and soybean, with a rye cover crop
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean_rye.why: It keeps the corn and soybean turns and adds a living cover over winter. Shown to compare.
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean_rye.evide: Iowa State recommends ending a cereal rye cover 10 to 14 days before planting corn. In Iowa State and Precision Sustainable Ag trials, corn planted green into rye yielded less than corn planted after the rye was ended at most sites (10 of 13 in 2021, 11 of 14 in 2022, 10 of 12 in 2023).
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean_rye.benef: A living cover over winter, when the soil is otherwise bare. Keeps the turns of corn and soybean.
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean_rye.unkno: How much water the rye uses before corn. The model cannot show it. The erosion rule for this option is not verified yet.
rotation.strategy.corn_soybean_rye.risks: Corn can yield less if the rye is ended too close to planting. Plan the end date of the rye around the corn planting date.
method.planting_window: FAO-56 water balance and growing degree days; one scenario per historical year. Dates tried: your date plus or minus 2 weeks, every 7 days. The window is the dates that score within 3 points of the best, widened by 3 days on each side. If it reaches the first or the last date tried, the dates beyond it were not tested.
method.hybrid_fit: Growing degree days (base 10 °C, cap 30 °C) to maturity vs. the first killing frost (−2 °C).
method.flowering_water: FAO-56 daily root-zone water balance and the Ky yield response to water (FAO-33). A year counts as short when the season's loss from water is 15 % or more, or water is 30 mm or more short around silking.
method.flowering_heat: Days with a high ≥ 35 °C from 10 days before to 10 days after silking.
method.frost: Frost ≤ 0 °C within 30 days of emergence, and a killing frost before maturity.
method.irrigation: Peak 7-day crop water use vs. system capacity times efficiency.
method.season_progress: MODIS NDVI green-up date (NDVI ≥ 0.5) vs. the field's own history.
method.waterlogging: Heaviest 3-day rain before silking vs. a threshold that depends on soil drainage.
method.field_zones: Median peak-season NDVI of several seasons from Sentinel-2 at 10 m; each part of the field is compared with the field's own median (less green: more than 5 % below it; greener: more than 5 % above it).
method.field_zones_sample: Invented sample zones, drawn only to show how the layer looks. No satellite data was used.
enso.weak: {now_phase}: {years} simulated past seasons had this phase. No clear difference on this field: {delta_pct} in relative yield against neutral years (clear needs 5 seasons and 3 points).
enso.moderate: {now_phase}: in simulated past seasons with this phase, relative yield on this field showed a moderate difference from neutral years ({delta_pct}).
enso.strong: {now_phase}: in simulated past seasons with this phase, relative yield on this field showed a large difference from neutral years ({delta_pct}).
pdf.title: Field report
pdf.history: History, El Niño, rotation and zones
pdf.zones_none: Zones inside the field are not available yet.
pdf.assumption.1: A future season is built from each historical year's weather at the same place (scenarios).
pdf.assumption.2: Soil water uses the FAO-56 daily balance and SSURGO soil properties.
pdf.assumption.3: Water-driven loss follows FAO-33 (Ky by stage); it is not a yield forecast.
pdf.assumption.4: Everything is computed in metric units and converted only for display.
pdf.disclaimer: This report supports the decisions of farmers and agronomists. It does not replace field scouting or local judgment.
pdf.mock: Sample data (no API): this report is not from a real computation.
